title: The whispered line
hook: "blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom" is whispered, except on Yom Kippur

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shema, said with a hand over the eyes. Your line was like the four fringes in one hand. Today, the line that comes right after, said under the breath.
screen: `LIKE THE FOUR FRINGES IN ONE HAND.`

segments.voice: Stand in a synagogue at the Shema and you'll hear six words said out loud, strong, sometimes sung. Then the room goes quiet. Lips are moving, but nobody's voice carries. A line is being said in a whisper. It's not in the Torah, and it isn't printed as part of the verse. And on one day a year, Yom Kippur, the whole room says it out loud.
screen: `SIX WORDS, OUT LOUD.` → `THEN A WHISPER.` → `ONCE A YEAR, ALOUD.`

segments.voice: The line is baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed: blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever and ever. The Talmud, in tractate Pesachim, tells where it comes from. Jacob lies dying, his twelve sons around him. He's afraid one of them has drifted from his faith. The sons answer with the words of the Shema, using his other name, Israel: hear, O Israel, our father, the LORD is our God, the LORD is one. Just as there is only one in your heart, so in ours. And Jacob, relieved, answers: blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever and ever. So the rabbis faced a puzzle. Should we say Jacob's line? Moses didn't write it in the Torah. Should we leave it out? Jacob said it. Their answer: say it, quietly. They compare it to a king's daughter who craved a spiced dish; to say so openly would embarrass her, to go without would hurt her, so her servants brought it to her in secret. A midrash tells another story: Moses overheard the line from the angels and brought it down, so on most days people say it softly, as something borrowed. But on Yom Kippur, when people are said to be like angels, they say it aloud. It has a Temple history, too. On Yom Kippur, when the high priest spoke God's name, the crowd answered with this very line.
screen: `BLESSED BE THE NAME OF HIS KINGDOM.` · `JACOB'S DEATHBED ANSWER.` · `SAY IT, BUT QUIETLY.` · `ALOUD ONLY ON YOM KIPPUR.` · then, large: `SOME WORDS ARE WHISPERED.`

segments.voice: Think of something true you don't usually say out loud: thanks you're too shy to give, a fragile hope, love you haven't spoken. Breathe with it for a while, then whisper it, barely a breath, so only you can hear. If you pray, you can whisper the line itself: baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed.
Baruch shem. Blessed be the name — the whispered line said right after the Shema, aloud only on Yom Kippur.
Your line: some words are whispered. The week ran from the call, through light, angels, great love, the corners and hear, to the whisper. See you tomorrow.
